## CHAPTER I

INTRODUCTION

This thesis is composed of a review of current literature and two manuscripts that are formatted for submission to scientific journals.  Chapter II outlines major findings and issues of wind farms’ environmental assessments.  It is composed of previous research and summarizes findings throughout the United States.  Chapter III is formatted for submission to The Wilson Journal of Ornithology, a publication of The Wilson Ornithological Society. This chapter explores potential habitat loss and degradation for breeding grassland birds as it pertains to visual and auditory sensitivity (i.e., wind turbines).  Chapter IV is written for submission to Biological Conservation.  In this chapter, I discuss bat collisions with turbines at the Oklahoma Wind Energy Center in northwestern Oklahoma and calculate conservative estimates of summertime collision mortality along with spatial distribution fatality analysis.

## CHAPTER II

LITERATURE REVIEW OF WILDLIFE IMPACT WIND RESEARCH

## **Wind Development**

With an increased cost of nonrenewable resources such as coal, natural gas, and oil, the development of alternative sources such as wind, solar, and geothermal energy has increased.  Of these major alternatives, wind development has shown the greatest strides in cost effectiveness and technological advancements (Bird et al. in press; Swisher et al _._ 2001).  Many European countries including The Netherlands, Denmark, England, Germany, and Spain currently convert wind energy to electricity.  Wind energy production spans every continent except Antarctica (American Wind Energy Association [AWEA] 2005), but even Antarctica has been evaluated for wind energy potential and feasibility (Teetz et al. 2003).

In the United States, wind energy production has increased dramatically since the development of Altamont Pass Wind Resource Area (APWRA) outside Livermore, CA in 1981 (Swisher et al. 2001; AWEA 2004).  Currently, utility companies in more than 30 states generate wind energy for a combined total of 9,149 megawatts (MW) which can supply energy to more than 2.7 million homes (AWEA 2006).

The Midwest (area between the Rocky Mountains and the Mississippi River) has experienced the greatest increase in wind development, with every state in this region containing commercially operated wind facilities (AWEA 2005).  Currently the most rapid area of development occurs in the Southern Great Plains (AWEA 2005).  By December 2005, Oklahoma installed 475 MW of wind generating capacity which is ranked fifth in the United States for installed wind capacity (Belyen and Real de Azua 2006).  Kansas and Nebraska are experiencing similar increases in wind development (Anonymous 2005; AWEA 2005a) with 180 MW proposed (AWEA 2005).  Wind

development will continue to accelerate as governments begin to grant subsidies and tax exemptions to major developers (Real de Azua 2006; Anonymous 2004; Menanteau et al _._ 2001; Migliore and Calvert 1999).

## **Direct Collision Mortality**

Despite research efforts evaluating avian turbine collisions since the 1980’s, the influence of this mortality on populations is unclear but probably low compared to mortality with other anthropogenic structures (Winkleman 1995).  Variability in collision mortality of birds and/or bats ranging from zero (Johnson et al. 2003) to an estimated 2092 (Kerns and Kerlinger 2004) suggests discrepancy across the nation possibly due to human sampling methods or as an artifact of geography (e.g., seasonal differences or weather events) (Morrison and Pollock 2003).  However, protocol and search biases are not consistent among all study projects, for example, searches that used linear transect versus radial transects.  Osborn et al. (2000) concluded mortality at the Buffalo Ridge Wind Resource Area, Minnesota to be only 12 fatalities of 11 species at 73 turbines in a single year (1994-1995).  At the APWRA, 439 fatalities of 31 species at 1,110 turbines were documented between 1998 and 2000 (Thelander et al. 2003) (Table 1).  The APWRA suggests nearly three times the mortality of Buffalo Ridge.

Potential influences of wind energy development on native wildlife (Johnson et al. 2000), especially related to bird and bat fatalities, have received increasing attention (Arnett et al _._ 2005; Johnson et al _._ 2003, 2002; Kern and Kerlinger 2004; Osborn et al _._ 2000).  Most research targets raptors and other soaring species as the major concern (Strickland et al. 2000; Thelander et al. 2003).  However, other species like waterfowl have been acknowledged as a concern, and in-flight avoidance behaviors have been

positively associated with turbines (Koford et al. 2004).  To mitigate collisions, use of GIS has been applied to previous work at APWRA (Thelander et al. 2003) and a forecasting model developed in order to reduce avian collision risk (Smallwood and Neher 2004).

Bats also collide with turbines (Table 2) but until 2003 research had suggested no serious population impacts to bats from collisions with wind turbines (Johnson et al _._ 2004, 2003; NWCC 2004; Osborn et al _._ 1996; Schmidt et al. 2003; Thelander et al. 2003).  This view changed when a West Virginia wind facility (Mountaineer Wind Resource Area) recorded hundreds of migratory bat fatalities, specifically _Lasiurus sp_ ., in a single year (Kerns and Kerlinger 2004; Williams 2003, 2004).  Since this phenomenon was documented, additional efforts to monitor bat mortality in the Ridge and Valley Region of the Central Appalachians have been pursued to better explain bat mortality (Arnett et al. 2005).

Wind turbine collisions primarily affect migratory bats such as the solitary treeroosting red ( _Lasiurus borealis_ ) and hoary ( _L. cinereus_ ) bats (Arnett et al. 2005, Johnson et al. 2003, Erickson et al. 2002, Kerns and Kerlinger 2004).  These species are typically found during migration times (August – October) and search effort is focused on these times.  Some research expresses a need for more searches to be conducted during spring and summer months (April – October) to understand temporal patterns (Arnett et al _._ 2005) and effects on resident populations (Arnett et al. 2005, Hoye 2005). Environmental organization and wind industry has suggested research into potential effects of collision mortality on maternity colonies as well as migrational populations

(Proceeding of the Wind Energy Bird/Bat Workshop 2004; Wind Power and Wildlife in Colorado Symposium and Workshop 2006).

Avian collision mortality has not only been documented in recent year at wind farms but have been documented for decades at lighthouses (Jones and Francis 2003), television towers (Avery and Clement 1972; Clark et al. 2005; Cochran and Graber 1958; Crawford 1981; Jones and Francis 2003), high tension lines (Coues 1876; Faanes 1987) and windows (Dunn 1993; Klem 1990, 1989; O’Connell 2001).  One on-line source (www.towerkill.com) suggests communications towers kill approximately five million birds annually in North America.  Window collision mortality may approach one billion fatalities per year in the United States (Klem 1990).  Some of these previous studies indicate differences in collision rates due to different migration patterns of species (early September versus late October) and weather events such as fog, rain, or high wind events (Clark et al _._ 2005; Cochran and Graber 1958; Crawford 1981; Dunn 1993; Jones and Francis 2003).  Collisions with these man-made structures are several orders of magnitude higher than wind turbine collisions (~30,000 avian kills annually; Erickson et al. 2001).  Avery (1979) suggested biological significance (species stability) of any avian species resulting from collision mortality with manmade structures is largely unknown because of a multitude of factors (e.g., total population size, natural mortality levels, and human related influences) and insufficient data.

## **Indirect Effects of Turbines**

Indirect effects of wind development on native wildlife pertaining to phenomena other than direct collisions have received increasing study (Johnson et al. 2002; Osborn et al. 2000); however, the bulk of this research effort has been directed towards avian

collisions with turbines (De Lucas et al. 2004; Johnson et al.2003, 2002, 2000; Koford et al. 2004; Osborn et al. 2000; Strickland et al. 2003; Thelander et al. 2003).  While some research has compared observations of flight behavior (Koford et al. 2004; Johnson et al. 2000a; Osborn et al. 1998; Smallwood and Neher 2004; Strickland et al. 2003; Urgoretz et al. 2003) and habitat use (Koford et al. 2004; Thelander et al. 2003) as an indirect measurement of potential avian collision rates, Johnson et al. (2000a) and Leddy et al. (1999) have tried to describe “ecological footprints” of disturbance around turbines that may degrade habitat suitability for breeding species.

Indirect measurements of avian turbine collision mortality have shown avian awareness of wind turbines.  Flight behavior studies indicate a significant alteration of flight path due to turbine presence (Koford et al. 2004; Morrison 1998; Osborn et al. 1998; Strickland et al. 2003) and specific species use difference landscape characteristics based on topography (Smallwood and Neher 2004).  Change in habitat use patterns by birds may be influenced by altered vegetation composition.  This can be attributed to construction of the turbines and maintenance of turbine pads, access roads, and associated areas that may change the food availability for some avian species (Thelander et al. 2003).  Finally, nest success may be negatively correlated with proximity to wind turbines.  Leddy et al. (1999) showed a decrease in breeding bird density within 180 meters of turbines.  These indirect factors may be more important to local bird and bat populations than direct collision mortality due to habitat loss and degradation especially in critical prairie environments (Fuhlendorf et al. 2002; Jackson 2002; Samson and Knopf 1994).  Rotenberry and Wiens (1980) measured vertical structure sensitivity of some

grassland species such as Western Meadowlark ( _Sturnella neglecta_ ), Dickcissel ( _Spiza americana_ ), and Grasshopper Sparrow ( _Ammodramus savannarum_ ).

## **Possible Knowledge Gaps**

Previous research has focused primarily on turbine collision mortality and flight characteristics of birds in order to reduce mortality at wind facilities.  In more recent years, research has focused on habitat degradation (Koford et al. 2004; Thelander et al. 2003) and avian breeding success (Johnson et al. 2000a; Leddy et al _._ 1999; Shaffer and Johnson 2004).  However, these indirect effects are more difficult to quantify, simply because there are multiple factors to consider (e.g., local habitat change, increased fragmentation by access roads, and visual and acoustical interference by the turbines). Species respond differently to these factors with some species being more tolerant (e.g., Eastern Meadowlark { _Sturnella magna_ }), others may be more sensitive (e.g., Lesser Prairie-Chicken ( _Tympanuchus pallidicinctus_ }).

Research on collision mortality needs to continue because there are still important issues that need to be better understood.  Predicting “hotspots” of avian and bat mortality will improve siting of wind facilities and turbines, thereby, minimizing direct impact. Summarizing fatalities across the nation (and global) (NWCC 2004) may help to monitor the effect of turbines as a human-related cause of mortality.

Much is unknown about the proximate interaction of birds and bats with turbines. Recently, Dooling (2002) published information that suggests that acoustical deterrents outside the range of human hearing will not function because of a narrower range of hearing in most birds.  Other mitigation efforts have not shown significant success such as “visual enhancement” (e.g., UV paint; Young et al. 2003a).  In terms of some bats,

their natural history remains incomplete, including details on diet, migration and foraging movements.  It has also been suggested that in some cases bats, are small enough to get caught in a low-pressure vortex at the tips of turbine blades which can cause internal bleeding from ruptured veins (Anonymous 2006; Winkleman 1995).  So how do bats intimately interact with turbines?  What causes birds and bats to collide with these structures?  And finally, what will happen as more turbines are erected?  These represent questions that still need to be addressed.

## CHAPTER III

WIND GENERATION OPERATION EFFECTS ASSOCIATED WITH BREEDING

HABITAT USE BY GRASSLAND BIRDS

## **Abstract**

Habitat degradation, loss, and other indirect effects of wind farms on breeding birds are poorly understood.  From May through July in 2004 and 2005, I studied breeding songbirds at a 102-megawatt (MW) wind farm in northwestern Oklahoma.  My objectives for this project were to (1) determine the potential density of singing males that were holding territories in the vicinity of the OWEC, (2) derive density estimates for common breeding species accounting for species specific detection probabilities, and (3) compare density estimates of breeding birds with increasing distance from the nearest turbine.  I documented a total of 80 species within 10 km of the wind farm using sixminute point counts.  I tested twenty-seven species for density differences, in terms of singing males, relative to the proximity of wind turbines.  Only four species (Greater Roadrunner [ _Geococcyx californianus_ ], Mourning Dove [ _Zenaida macroura_ ], Northern Mockingbird [ _Mimus polyglottos_ ], and Western Meadowlark [ _Sturnella neglatca_ ]) indicated a significant avoidance effect of which Western Meadowlark was the only grassland obligate.  Conservation priority species such as Painted Bunting ( _Passerina ciris_ ) and Bewick’s Wren ( _Thryomanes bewickii_ ) did not have a significant avoidance effect.  Species may respond to habitat variables such as patch size or perimeter-area ratio more strongly than presence of turbines which makes it difficult to conclude specific tendencies in density trends as it pertains to turbine distance.

## **Introduction**

As the number of wind power generation facilities has increased in recent years, the potential detrimental effects of wind energy development on native wildlife,

especially avian collisions with towers and turbines, has received increasing attention (Osborn _et al_ . 2000, Kingsley and Whittam 2001, Dooling 2002, Johnson _et al_ . 2002, DeLucas _et al_ . 2004).  In addition to direct collision mortality, some species may vacate otherwise suitable areas where turbines have been erected.  Recent evidence from radiotagged Lesser Prairie-Chickens ( _Tympanuchus pallidicinctus_ ) suggest that they seldom approach closer than several hundred meters to anthropogenic features like transmission lines and improved roads (Robert Robel, _pers. comm._ ).  Certain songbirds may respond similarly to tall structures in otherwise open habitat.  At the Buffalo Ridge Wind Resource Area in Minnesota, Leddy _et al_ . (1999) found that density of eleven grassland singing males increased beyond 180 m from turbine strings.

The potential avoidance of otherwise suitable habitat that contains wind turbines merits additional study.  Determining which species are most likely to abandon sites of wind development and exhibit avoidance behaviors in these habitats are important conservation issues.  Few studies have examined the effects of spatial bird distributions, population densities, and nest success.  These factors could create conditions for some species in which the “realized footprint” or area of disturbance around a wind turbine is considerably larger than the area physically disturbed to erect the tower.  Johnson and Igl (2001) reported that at least seven grassland breeding birds required patches of contiguous habitat significantly larger than the individual home range.  Could area sensitive grassland breeders stand to lose significant amounts of habitat where wind turbines are erected?

To illustrate, many songbirds will likely encounter unsuitable nesting habitat around the base of wind turbines due to the presence of a turbine and associated

maintenance pad around the turbine.  For example, if this permanently disturbed area is a circle of 20 m radius around the tower, then this area is approximately 0.13 ha.  In a wind development area that includes 100 turbines, the minimum habitat lost to nesting songbirds would be approximately 13 ha (not including access roads, electrical substation areas, other service or administration buildings and parking areas).  If, however, a species tends to avoid a larger area around each turbine, then the potential habitat loss is correspondingly greater.  A species that will not nest within 100 m of active turbines (such as Sedge Wren from Leddy _et al._ 1999) will lose proportionately more nesting habitat, in this case 314 ha per 100 turbines.  In regions where habitat loss and fragmentation figure prominently in the conservation of native species, such as mixed grass prairie, any activities that further degrade native habitats should be closely scrutinized.  Some estimates suggest that more than 99% of the original North American native prairie has been lost (Samson and Knopf 1994) resulting in grassland birds declining more severely and over a longer period of time than any other bird taxa through the 20[th] century (Knopf 1992).

While some species may abandon habitat in proximity to wind turbines, others may be unaffected or even derive unknown benefits from nesting near turbines.  For example, Leddy et al. (1999) described ten of eleven species occurred in Conservation Reserve Program fields regardless of turbine presence.  Because this issue has not been studied in detail, however, we do not have enough information to predict these indirect effects of wind development.  The issue is, therefore, not a major consideration in the siting of new wind development projects, and it is difficult for natural resource professionals to gauge the cumulative effects of wind development in a given area.  From

a business standpoint, the wind power industry is currently unable to predict how the indirect effects of wind development on native birds may influence public relations, investments, or future regulations.

From May through July in 2004 and 2005, I studied the effects of wind operation on breeding songbirds at FPL Energy’s 102-megawatt Oklahoma Wind Energy Center (OWEC) in Harper and Woodward counties (Fig. 1).  At least three regional conservation priority species (Lesser Prairie-Chicken, Scissor-tailed Flycatcher [ _Tyrannus forficatus_ ], and Cassin’s Sparrow [ _Aimophila cassinii_ ]) are known to breed in the vicinity of the OWEC (Reinking 2004, Carter et al. 2000, Baumgartner and Baumgartner 1992; taxonomy follows AOU 1998).  Additional species that are priorities in this area, such as Painted Bunting ( _Passerina ciris_ ) and Bewick’s Wren ( _Thryomanes bewickii_ ) are common at the OWEC site.

I investigated the indirect effect of breeding habitat use by grassland bird at the OWEC.  My objectives for this project were to (1) determine the potential density of singing males that were holding territories in the vicinity of the OWEC, (2) derive density estimates for common breeding species accounting for species specific detection probabilities, and (3) compare density estimates of breeding birds with increasing distance from the nearest turbine.

## **Methods**

## _Site Description._

The OWEC site was developed in an agricultural landscape used predominantly for wheat production and cattle grazing.  The OWEC is located in the Rolling Red Plains

of the North American Bird Conservation Initiative’s Central Mixed-Grass Prairie Bird Conservation Region (Pashley _et al._ 2000) (Fig 1). Approximately 34 of 68 turbines have been erected along seasonally dry riparian ravines that feed the Cimarron River.  The ravines support wooded vegetation typical of the region, dominated by eastern redcedar ( _Juniperus virginiana_ ) , eastern cottonwood ( _Populus deltoides_ ), American elm ( _Ulmus americana_ ), and hackberry ( _Celtis laevigata_ ) (Tyrl _et al._ 2002).  Due largely to decades of fire suppression in Oklahoma (Fuhlendorf _et al._ 1997), eastern redcedar from the ravines has become established on the upland pastures over much of the OWEC area.

The remaining turbines were erected in crop fields or pastures supporting native prairie vegetation.  Topography in these areas is generally level.  In pastures, little bluestem ( _Schizachyrium scoparium_ ) dominates the vegetation cover and patches of sand plum ( _Prunus angustifolia_ ) and sand sage ( _Artemesia filifolia_ ) are conspicuous elements on sandy soils.  Groves of smaller trees (e.g., soapberry [ _Sapindus drummondii_ ] and black locust [ _Robinia pseudoacacia_ ]) also occur in these fields (Tyrl _et al._ 2002).  Crop field were planted with either wheat or rye, and early in the season (May) and after harvest (July) cattle were allowed to graze in these fields.

_Site Reconnaissance and Sampling Design._

Among my first tasks was to determine the most appropriate sampling technique to apply to the study site.  Prior to the start of field work, I knew that the basic sampling unit would be a fixed-radius, timed point count to which I could apply removal models to correct abundance estimates for detection probabilities of species (Petit _et al._ 1995, Savard and Hooper 1995, Farnsworth _et al_ . 2002).  I used these detection probabilities

along with raw abundance and sampled area information to derive estimates of breeding density for multiple species.

I considered strip transects, grid sampling, and point counts along transects as sampling arrays.  Several factors contributed to my decision.  First, turbines in all cover types were located along sand or gravel access roads, with sparsely vegetated construction pads occupying approximately 0.25 ha around each tower.  My ability to compare densities of breeding birds at varying distances to wind turbines was predicated on my ability to replicate habitat conditions as closely as possible among transects placed at the different distances.  To permit comparisons among counts conducted adjacent to and at varying distances from the towers, all sampling locations needed to include some amount of secondary road and/or bare ground because of access road located next to all turbine strings.  A second factor that shaped my design involved logistics: at least one private landowner who allowed me to conduct field work on his land prohibited me from sampling away from the access roads causing me to remain on these roads to conduct point counts.  The restriction to roads steered me toward a linear sampling scheme (e.g., transects) and away from a gridded design.

For the sampling grain, I conducted a series of test counts to determine the effective listening radius in the site terrain.  Using an optical rangefinder, I judged counts at 50- and 100-m radii yielded too few registrations within the radius relative to beyond it.  A 200-m sampling radius (approximately 12.6 ha sampling area) provided multiple “countable” individuals at each point, while retaining confidence on my part that I was recording close to 100% of all singing males within the count circle.  To minimize the possibility of individuals being recorded in adjacent count circles (i.e., “double-

counted”), I separated count points by 400 m as recommended by Ralph _et al._ (1995). With 400 meters between adjacent points, I thus needed access to 1200 meters of homogeneous, roaded habitat to accommodate four counts per transect, which would result in an effective sampling area of approximately 50 ha per transect (Fig. 2).

At the OWEC, five turbine arrays spanning at least 1200 m of a homogeneous cover type were available as sampling transects adjacent to operational turbines.  Of these, three turbine strings occurred in mixed pasture and eastern redcedar scrub along dry ravines that drain the area; one was located entirely within a wheat field, and the other one in native prairie.  I identified and established additional transects approximately 1-5 km to the nearest turbine (intermediate) and 5-10 km away (distant) using a detailed topological map (DeLorme 2003) and site reconnaissance.  In addition, I sampled from 9 intermediates (3 each in mixed, crop, and prairie cover), and 12 distant (four each in mixed, crop, and prairie cover) transects for a total of 26 transect counts (Fig. 3). I was limited to three-points at one transect; all others included four sampling points, for a total of 103, 200-m point count stations at and in the vicinity of the OWEC.  The effective sampling area was 12.56 ha/point X 103 points = 1293.68 ha.

_Field Sampling Protocols._

I conducted point counts during early morning hours (roughly 0530 – 0930 CDT) under dry conditions with relatively light winds (< 32 kph).  Counts for singing males followed standard songbird sampling procedures recommended in Ralph _et al._ (1995) with some modifications.  Recently, several authors have pointed out the need to account for sampling biases (Link and Sauer 1998) by incorporating some method that estimates detection probabilities in count data (Thompson 2002).  Because I was the only observer,

there was no observer bias.  This allowed me to apply a removal model and address detection bias for various species.  Options for detection probability estimation include distance sampling (Rosenstock _et al._ 2002, Diefenbach _et al._ 2003), double sampling (Nichols _et al_ . 2000, Bart and Earnst 2002, Pollock _et al_ . 2002), and the _post hoc_ application of count removal models (Farnsworth _et al._ 2002).  Count removal models provide the greatest flexibility in the field, requiring only that individual birds are recorded in discrete time bands.  For the more commonly encountered species, I was able to calculate species-specific detection probabilities (Table 1) using the SURVIV program (Farnsworth _et al._ 2002).  I used these probabilities to correct for species detection differences in estimates of breeding males.  For those species that were less frequently encountered, I estimated density with an assumed default detection probability of 1.0.

The transect counts and associated calculations of detection probability are designed to provide accurate estimates of richness, abundance, and density of breeding birds in the sampled area.  I collected data on any individual of any species detected, but limited density calculations to data from singing, calling, or visually displaying male Passerines and allies holding territories on the sampled area (i.e., within 200 m of the center point). To ensure that I recorded individuals attempting to breed rather than migrants in passage, I restricted sampling to the period from 24 May to 15 July, i.e., after most transients have passed through the area but before territorial display behaviors break down and post-breeding dispersal becomes widespread (e.g., Anders _et al_ . 1998).  I recognize that June sampling likely missed first breeding attempts of early breeders such as Northern Cardinals ( _Cardinalis cardinalis_ ), but sampling much before the end of May would have resulted in the detection of many species that did not breed in the study area.

To increase confidence that I recorded breeding individuals rather than transients, I sampled all transects twice during the sampling period in 2004 and three times in 2005. Sampling rounds were separated by at least seven days to provide some confidence that the birds detected were actually holding territories in the sampled area.  I determined richness as the maximum number of species recorded from both samples of a given transect.  I calculated abundance and density as mean values for each transect over the two sampling periods.

_Data Preparation._

Density estimates for all species detected on more than 25 individual counts were modified according to detection probability as determined through the use of count removal models in the SURVIV program provided by the USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center (Farnsworth _et al_ . 2002).  Because my field sampling relied on sixminute point counts divided into three, two-minute intervals, I could not use the prefabricated SURVIV code designed for ten-minute counts divided into three, two, and five-minute intervals, respectively.  I, therefore, modified the SURVIV program to accommodate my difference in sampling intervals.

_Vegetation Sampling._

I characterized the vegetation along each transect with 10, systematically identified sampling plots for each of 26 transects.  At each point along the transect, I randomly selected a direction (left or right) to place a vegetation sampling plot up to 50 m from the transect center line.  At each sampling point, I determined vegetation height density with a Robel pole (Robel _et al_ . 1970).  In addition, I established a 1 m[2] sampling plot with a random toss Daubenmire frame (Daubenmire 1959). Within the sampling plot,

I identified all vegetation to species, and visually estimated the percent cover of each, as well as that of exposed soil, rock, etc.  To assess the relative amount of eastern redcedar cover, I applied a point-center-quarter sampling technique to each vegetation sampling plot (Cottam and Curtis 1956, 1949).  This method permitted calculation of stem density per transect.

_Analysis._

Data analysis focused first on establishing the similarity of vegetation conditions within cover type designations and the appropriateness of my habitat replicate transects at 1-5 and 5-10 km from the turbines.  I used a one-way classification for analysis of variance to compare variables of visual obstruction and redcedar stem density (via pointcenter-quarter method).

For analysis, numbers of singing males / 100 ha were adjusted for those species with calculated detection probabilities for all three distance categories.  I tested for homogeneity of variance for each response variable, number of singing males / 100 ha, using a Levene’s Test.  The response variable within a habitat type was analyzed using a General Linear Model (GLM) with factors of year, distance from turbine, and an interaction of year*distance.  A separate GLM for each year was completed for those response variables that indicated a significant interaction.  I conducted regression analysis of each response variable using distance as a continuous variable predictor (distance obtained using remote sensing via ArcView 3.3).  I graphed the regressions that showed a significant interaction, year, or distance effect.  I included in the graphs the corresponding R[2] -value.  I used α < 0.05 to indicate statistical significance; all analyses were carried out with Minitab statistical software (Minitab 1995).

## **Results**

## _Vegetation Results_

Within habitat types, vegetation sampling revealed similarities in species present and percent cover.  I identified 33 species of grasses and forbs in 528 vegetation plots at 26 sites in 2004 and 2005 (Table 2).  Plant species richness was highest in mixed fields (26 spp), followed by prairie (21 spp) and crop fields (14 spp).  I interpret the greater species richness of mixed fields relative to native prairie to the unequal sampling of the two habitats:  I sampled from 18 more plots on mixed transects than I sampled on prairie transects.

Foliage height density (measured via visual obstruction) was similar in crop and prairie plots, but significantly denser within mixed plots (Fig. 4).  As expected, mixed plots also supported significantly more stem densities of eastern redcedar (Fig. 5).

Vegetative cover differed among the three habitat types.  Wheat cover was significantly different and greater in crop fields than in prairie or mixed fields in 2004 and 2005 (F2,257 = 70.98, P < 0.001 [2004] and F2,253 = 132.05, P < 0.001 [2005]) (Fig. 6). In 2005, I recorded significantly more percent wheat cover than in 2004 (F1, 514 = 17.36, P < 0.001) (Fig. 6).  Percent cover in grasses differed among all three habitats in 2004 (F2,257 = 37.31, P < 0.001).  Confidence intervals for the difference in pairwise comparisons among crop, prairie, and mixed did not include zero.  In 2005, percent cover of grasses was similar in prairie and mixed habitats, and these two categories were significantly different and greater than the grass cover in crop plots (F2,253 = 63.59, P < 0.001) (Fig. 7).  Grasses occupied a greater percent cover of sampling plots in 2004 (F1, 514[ = 19.47, P < 0.001) (Fig.7).  For more specific information on vegetative sampling, ]

## see Appendix B.

## _Avian Results_

I identified 80 species of birds in the study area (includes the OWEC and off-site sampling transects) from May through July in 2004 and 2005 (Appendix A, Table 1).  Of the 80 total species encountered, I documented 66 during point count samples.  These included a core group of species that are common in the study area (Table 3), as well as species that might have been encountered only once over two years of study, of which there were 15.  I recorded the species in Table 3 frequently enough (at least 25 times) to be included in calculations of detection probability that permitted an adjusted estimate of breeding density in terms of number of singing males / 100 ha.  The 43 species in Table 4 were not encountered frequently enough to permit detection-adjusted estimates of breeding density.  Appendix A, Tables 2 and 3 list species by habitat types and turbine distance, respectively.

There was no significant regression trend of breeding density in relation to turbine distance for 71 individual regressions on the species listed in Table 1.  Several open country species, including Horned Lark ( _Eremophila alpestris_ ), Killdeer ( _Charadrius vociferous_ ), Dickcissel ( _Spiza americana_ ), and Cassin’s Sparrow did not reveal any consistent pattern in breeding density related to turbine proximity (Fig. 8).  Conservation priority species such as Painted Bunting and Bewick’s Wren were also apparently unaffected by the presence of wind turbines on their breeding territories (Fig. 9).

Ten of 59 GLM analyses had a significant distance tendency with both years combined (Table 5).  Within mixed eastern redcedar habitats, Northern Mockingbird had the only significant interaction (p = 0.02) between year and distance.  Separating this

species by year, 2004 indicated a significant difference among distances (Table 6). Fourteen species (AMCR, BEWR, BGGN, COGO, EAKI, EAME, GCFL, GRRO, GRSP, LASP, NOCA, NOMO, YBCU, and RWBL [see Appendix B, Table 4 for species name]) had a significant main effect (year) (Tables 6 and 7).  With these separated by year, only Northern Mockingbird, Greater Roadrunner, Grasshopper Sparrow, and Eastern Meadowlark had a significant distance effect (Tables 6 and 7).

Eleven species (NOBO, GRRO, MODO, NOMO, STFL, NOCA, GRSP, FISP, WEME, and BHCO) had significant regression trends during 2004 and 2005 combined and were plotted along the distance continuum (Fig. 10, 11, 12).  Of these ten species, four (GRRO, MODO, NOMO, and WEME) occurred at higher density further from the turbines.  Western Meadowlark was the only grassland obligate to have higher density further from the turbines.  Six species (NOCA, GRSP, FISP, BHCO, NOBO, and SCFL) all occurred at higher density close to turbines.  Northern cardinal was the only woodland species to have higher density close to the turbines.  For those species that had significant year effects in the GLM, I ran regressions for each by year.  Three species (NOMO, GCFL, and GRRO) occurred at higher density further from the turbines but only during a single year (Tables 6 and 7; Fig. 13).

## **Discussion**

Identification of suitable replicate sampling areas at varying distances to the OWEC turbines proved challenging.  I erred on the side of replicating vegetation cover as closely as was possible, but forced to sacrifice some similarity in topographic relief. Several of the 5-10 km transects were located north and east of the OWEC site, where the

land sloped toward the Cimarron River.  As a result, transects in all three distance categories occupied different elevations from adjacent (654 m) to distant (514 m).

Visual obstruction increased from crop to prairie to mixed habitat types (Fig 4).  I attribute this primarily to the corresponding increase in redcedar stem density (Fig 5) and grasses (Fig. 7).  I attribute differences in grass and wheat measurements between the two years to a difference in the dates during which I collected these data.  In 2004, all vegetation sampling was conducted in July, by which time warm season grasses had grown considerably and wheat had been harvested.  I sampled earlier (June) in 2005, at which time a standing crop of wheat persisted and the phenology of prairie grasses was not advanced as in July.  This may confound breeding bird composition and vegetation measurements since I conducted most point count surveys with standing wheat and/or rye.  Some species like Red-winged Blackbirds use the vertical structure of grasses and crops to display and build nests (Yasukawa and Searcy 1995) while other species like Horned Larks use bare soil on which to nest (Beason 1995).

Bird composition changed according to habitat type.  In some areas where transects crossed riparian headwater ravines, the habitat character varied from pasture with scattered cedars, to cedar and grass savanna, to cedar-dominated riparian forest with a canopy approximately 5-15 m high.  These areas supported woodland birds at the OWEC.  Included in these woodland birds were conservation priority species such as Painted Buntings and Bewick’s Wrens (Fig. 9).

The basic unit for comparison in my study was breeding density, expressed as the number of singing or calling individuals (typically males) per 100 ha.  I adjusted singing male estimates only for those species with computed detection probabilities at all three

distance categories (Table 1).  The detection probabilities varied with respect to distance, however, the purpose of these past probabilities is to account for bias associated with local conditions (Farnsworth et al. 2002); so variation is expected.  At my sites, some transects were along pastures being actively grazed.  The presence of cattle moving and grazing close to me during point count surveys at a single site may have reduced my detection probability more than habitat variables.  This may have accounted for differences among species and turbine proximity, but there was no consistence relationship between turbine proximity and detection probability.

Differences in GLM and regression analyses were due to different F-test statistics. This resulted in ten analyses being significantly different in the categorical distance variable in the GLM.  Regression analyses used a continuous distance variable and resulted in eleven significant trends (Table 5).  The same was true when year was separated for those species that indicated a significant main effect of year (Tables 6 and

7).  In addition, a GLM uses least squares estimation to obtain the F-statistic while a regression uses maximum likeliness estimation (Neter et al. 1990).  Different computational methods did show some discrepancy in p-values and final results. However, my interpretation of trends relies more on the regression analysis because of the predicting factor, distance, being continuous and the ability to visualize the amount of variation in the data (i.e., noise).  I also suspect that variation increased in GLM analyses due to consolidating distances into categories.

Regression analyses of both years together had increasing trends for four species (GRRO, MODO, NOMO, and GCFL) with low conservation priority status (Fig. 10, 11, 12) (Rocky Mountain Bird Observatory 2005).  Three species (NOCA, BHCO, and

NOBO) had decreasing trends with increasing distance from the turbines and have low conservation priority status (Rocky Mountain Bird Observatory 2005).  These birds usually use vertical structure and nest (exception Brown-headed Cowbird) in shrubs or trees.

Three species of regional concern (Rocky Mountain Bird Observatory 2005) had decreasing regression trends with increasing distance from turbines.  Western Meadowlark was the only bird of regional concern (Rocky Mountain Bird Observatory 2005) that had higher numbers of singing male density with respect to distance. Microhabitat around the wind farm may have had more influence on density estimates rather than the presence of turbines.  These increased densities may be an artifact of spatial heterogeneity and patch size.

Although we did not investigate patch size or perimeter-area ratios, these factors do influence bird assemblages on a landscape (Helzer and Jelinski 1999; Rotenberry and Wiens 1990).  Species respond differently to these variables.  For example, Field Sparrows are more tolerant to vertical structures and presence of brushy pastures (Carey et al. 1994), whereas Western Meadowlarks prefer larger and more contiguous grassland habitats (Helzer and Jelinski 1999) and are negatively correlated to vertical structure (Rotenberry and Wiens 1990).  Both prairie and crop fields were larger at several of my distant transects while the only crop and prairie habitat at adjacent transect were less than a half mi[2] .  Helzer and Jelinski (1999) suggested a negative metrics relationship to increased perimeter-area ratio for grasshopper sparrow; however, my data suggests that Grasshopper Sparrows may have responded to some unaccounted variable with only one

relatively small crop patch adjacent to the turbine in which my sampling transect was located.

If patch size and perimeter-area ratios influenced some species, then it did not significantly influence other species of regional or continental concern such as the Painted Bunting and Bewick’s Wren.  These species were evenly represented at all distances from the wind farm (Fig. 9).  Cassin’s Sparrow, on the other hand, had two sites that held high numbers of singing males.  These two sites, at intermediate distance from the nearest turbine, may have caused a loss to any trend.  The sites were characterized by the transect bisecting a group of small hills consisting of sand sage patches.  These were the only two prairie transects with this type of topography and may not have been replicated at the site adjacent to the turbines.  Since other factors such as habitat may have a stronger influence on Cassin’s Sparrow, I can not speculate as to whether turbine presence is also affecting habitat use.

## **Conclusions**

Because my sampling grain (200 m radius point count) was more coarse than Leddy _et al_ . (1999), I am unable to comment on avoidance that may have occurred at the finer spatial scales used in that study, i.e., within 200 m of turbines.  Instead, I focused my efforts on a scale at which avoidance of turbines may realistically have been expected to influence open country birds: within “earshot” or “eyeshot” of turbines.  For most species the presence of turbines did not affect the breeding habitat use.  However, several species did respond to distance, and Western Meadowlark was the only grassland obligate to be positively correlated with increasing turbine distance.  Field Sparrow,
